_readme: Scale suggestions for every chord. Edit this file to change what the analyzer suggests.
RULES ARE TRIED TOP TO BOTTOM; THE FIRST RULE WHOSE 'when' MATCHES WINS. Put specific rules above general ones.
'when' keys (all optional, all must match; leave 'when' out for a catch-all):
quality      chord qualities: MAJOR MINOR DIMINISHED AUGMENTED SUS2 SUS4 MAJOR6 MINOR6 MAJOR7 MINOR7 DOMINANT7
MINOR_MAJOR7 HALF_DIMINISHED7 DIMINISHED7 AUGMENTED7 MAJOR7_SHARP5 DOMINANT7_SUS4
function     TONIC SUBDOMINANT DOMINANT SECONDARY_DOMINANT TRITONE_SUBSTITUTION DIMINISHED_PASSING MODAL_INTERCHANGE UNCLASSIFIED
degree       root above the local tonic: I bII II bIII III IV #IV V bVI VI bVII VII (case never matters, so 'II' means ii and II)
resolution   MAJOR, MINOR or NONE: where the chord resolves (down a fifth; for dominants also down a half step)
mode         MAJOR or MINOR (the local key)
alterations  tones the chord must contain (it may contain others too), e.g. ['#11'] or ['b9','b13']
exactAlterations  the chord's alterations must be exactly these and nothing else, e.g. ['b9'] means 'just a b9'
'scales' maps a scale name to its formula (scale degrees against a major scale, e.g. Dorian = 1 2 b3 4 5 6 b7).
'origin': 'spec' = from the original rule table; 'added' = an addition. 'note' (optional) is a free-text comment.
Suggestions are listed in rank order (first = first choice).

suggestions.reason: 7alt implies b9, #9, b5 and b13 together: the altered scale contains all of them
Symmetric alternative with b9 and #9; sounds a little less 'inside' than altered

rules.note: Author's rule: a dominant with only a b9 (7b9) takes half-whole diminished, even when it resolves to a minor chord.

suggestions.reason: A dominant with only a b9 (7b9): half-whole diminished has the b9 and keeps the natural 13
Contains both the b9 and the #11 written in the symbol, plus a natural 13
A dominant 7 with a #11: Lydian dominant has the #4 and a b7
Standard choice over a tritone substitution (bII7): it contains the tones that blend with the chord it replaces
Resolving to a minor chord: the b9 and b13 point to the minor tonic
Maximum tension before resolving to the minor chord
Milder option: keeps the natural 9 but still has the minor-flavoured b13
The symbol asks for a b13 and nothing else altered
Standard choice over a dominant 7 resolving to a major chord
Adds tension (b9, #9, b5, b13) before the resolution
bVII7 (the 'backdoor' dominant) usually takes Lydian dominant
Plain alternative that stays closest to the chord
Default for a dominant 7 chord that does not resolve in a recognised way
A 7#5 chord is built from whole-tone tones
Alternative with more tension
Suspended dominant: Mixolydian contains the natural 4 and b7

rules.note: Author's rule: iiø7 in a minor key takes Locrian #2 first. (In a major key viiø7 keeps Locrian first, below.)

suggestions.reason: Standard choice over the iiø7 of a minor key: the natural 9 fits the key, where plain Locrian's b9 would clash
Plain Locrian: the mode built on the chord itself
The scale built on the chord: m7b5 is the Locrian chord
Same, with a natural 9 (softer than plain Locrian)

Symmetric scale that contains the diminished triad
mMaj7 is the tonic chord of melodic minor
